questions.stem: Which are the three syllabus purposes of data visualisation?
options: Simplifying understanding, telling a story, highlighting significant results
questions.explanation: Use these exact words in an exam. Additional purposes worth naming for depth: exploration vs explanation, monitoring KPIs, comparison, forecasting and persuasion.

questions.stem: Pre-attentive attributes are visual properties that:
options: Are processed almost instantly, before conscious attention
Describe the data's level of measurement
questions.explanation: Position, length, size, colour, shape and orientation are perceived in under a quarter of a second. Position and length are the most accurately judged — which is why bar charts beat pie charts.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to compare total sales across 15 product categories with long names. The best chart is:
questions.explanation: Bar (horizontal) accommodates long category labels legibly, and 15 slices would make a pie unreadable. The axis must start at zero for a length-encoded comparison.

questions.stem: Which chart is most appropriate for showing the relationship between two continuous variables?
questions.explanation: Scatter plot — Adding a third variable via marker size makes it a bubble chart; adding colour encodes a category.

questions.stem: A histogram differs from a bar chart because it:
options: Shows the distribution of a continuous variable in bins, with no gaps between bars
questions.explanation: Bar charts compare discrete categories; histograms show the shape of a distribution — skew, spread and bimodality that a mean conceals.

questions.stem: A choropleth map of total COVID cases by region is misleading unless the data is:
questions.explanation: An un-normalised choropleth mostly maps where people live. Rates per 100,000 make regions comparable.

questions.stem: Which visualisation best shows part-to-whole composition changing over time?
options: Stacked area or stacked bar chart
questions.explanation: A pie is a single moment only. Stacked area/bar shows both the total and the changing mix — though comparing non-baseline bands across time is genuinely hard for readers.

questions.stem: A box plot is preferred over a bar of means when you want to show:
questions.explanation: "Bar of means" hides everything about distribution — two groups with identical means can have wildly different spreads and outliers.

questions.stem: The main criticism of pie charts is that:
options: Humans judge angles and areas poorly, so small differences are hard to compare
questions.explanation: Keep to ≤5 slices, order them, label directly — or use a bar chart instead. Position/length beats angle/area for accuracy of perception.

questions.stem: Which is the key difference between an infographic and a dashboard?
options: An infographic is interactive; a dashboard is static
Infographics can only use bar charts
An infographic is a static, designer-curated narrative; a dashboard is dynamic, live and user-filtered
questions.explanation: Infographic = one story, one audience, one moment. Dashboard = ongoing monitoring, user-driven interrogation, live data. A report is the detailed written analysis with methodology.

questions.stem: A "big number" KPI tile is most effective when it:
options: Is paired with a comparison — versus target, versus last period, or a trend sparkline
questions.explanation: A number without a reference point carries no meaning. "$1.2M" says nothing; "$1.2M, 8% above target, up from $1.05M" says everything.

questions.stem: A word cloud should be described as:
options: An impressionistic view of term frequency, not a quantitative tool
questions.explanation: Word size maps to frequency but layout is arbitrary, long words look bigger, and context and sentiment are lost. Fine for a first look; indefensible as evidence.

questions.stem: Small multiples are preferred over a single multi-series line chart when:
options: There are many series that would overlap into a "spaghetti chart"
The chart must be printed in black and white
questions.explanation: A grid of identically scaled mini-charts preserves comparability while removing overplotting. Shared axes are essential or the comparison is false.

questions.stem: A Sankey diagram is best used to show:
options: Flow and its magnitude between stages or categories
questions.explanation: Band width encodes volume — ideal for customer journey drop-off, energy flow or budget allocation.

questions.stem: In choosing a chart, the first question to ask is:
options: What question is the audience trying to answer, and what is the data's level of measurement?
Which chart type is newest in the software?
How much screen space is available?
questions.explanation: Chart choice follows from the analytical question and the data type. Working the other way — picking a chart then finding data for it — is how misleading visuals get made.

questions.stem: "Q4 revenue is forecast at $1.8M ± 8%" is an example of which level of analytics?
questions.explanation: Predictive — what will happen. Descriptive = what happened; diagnostic = why; prescriptive = what we should do about it.

questions.stem: "Shift $40,000 of marketing spend to the underperforming region" is:
questions.explanation: Prescriptive — recommending an action. It sits at the top of the value ladder and demands the highest data quality and model confidence.

questions.stem: Most enterprise dashboards stop at descriptive analytics. To climb to predictive, the enterprise most needs:
options: Sufficient clean historical data, stable underlying conditions and modelling capability
questions.explanation: Naming which level a system reaches, and what would be needed to advance one level, is a reliable way to earn marks in an evaluate question.

questions.stem: A repeating pattern of higher sales every December is:
questions.explanation: Seasonality — Failing to account for it makes December-to-January comparisons meaningless — one of the classic cherry-picking traps in stimulus questions.

questions.stem: Predictive analytics requires all of the following except:
options: Guaranteed causal relationships between all variables
questions.explanation: Useful prediction can rest on stable correlation. The caution is that a purely correlational model breaks precisely when the underlying conditions shift.

questions.stem: GPUs transformed data analytics primarily because they:
options: Store more data than hard drives
Perform massively parallel matrix computation, enabling deep learning and fast large-scale analysis
questions.explanation: Parallel arithmetic is exactly what neural network training needs. TPUs and NPUs extend the idea; distributed clusters (Hadoop/Spark) scale it horizontally.

questions.stem: The most significant effect of collapsing storage costs on enterprise analytics has been:
options: Data must now be stored on tape
Enterprises retain raw historical data instead of aggregating it away, enabling retrospective analysis and ML training
questions.explanation: Cheap object storage made "keep everything, decide later" economically rational — which is what created both the data lake and the data swamp.

questions.stem: In-memory processing improves analytics by:
options: Removing the disk read bottleneck so queries return in seconds rather than minutes
questions.explanation: The consequence is behavioural, not just technical: analysis becomes interactive and exploratory, so an analyst can ask a follow-up question while still holding the thought.

questions.stem: The move from 4G to 5G most directly enables which change in visualisation?
options: Real-time streaming dashboards and mobile decision-making at the point of work
questions.explanation: High bandwidth and low latency make live operational dashboards usable in the field — on a factory floor, in a warehouse, in a vehicle.

questions.stem: The democratisation of analytics through self-service BI has which significant downside?
options: "Shadow BI" — proliferating unofficial reports with conflicting numbers and no governance
questions.explanation: When everyone can build a dashboard, everyone can build a different answer to the same question. Governance — certified datasets, agreed measure definitions — is the counterweight.

questions.stem: In an OLAP cube, "sales revenue" is a:
questions.explanation: Measure (fact) — the number being analysed. Time, product, store and customer are dimensions, each with a hierarchy.

questions.stem: Restricting an OLAP cube to a single value on one dimension (e.g. year = 2026) is:
questions.explanation: Slice — one dimension fixed, producing a single flat sheet from the cube.

questions.stem: Selecting 2026 and NSW/VIC and Laptops from a cube is:
questions.explanation: Dice — constraining several dimensions at once to produce a smaller sub-cube.

questions.stem: Moving from Year → Quarter → Month is:
questions.explanation: Drill-down — descending a hierarchy to more detail. The reverse (Month → Quarter → Year) is roll-up.

questions.stem: Swapping the row and column dimensions to view the same data differently is:
questions.explanation: Pivot (rotate) — Same data, new perspective — the operation that gives pivot tables their name.

questions.stem: MOLAP compared with ROLAP:
options: MOLAP queries the relational warehouse directly and is slower
MOLAP pre-aggregates into a cube, giving fastest queries but heavier storage and refresh lag
questions.explanation: ROLAP queries the relational store directly — handles larger data, slower response. HOLAP hybridises: pre-aggregate the hot summaries, query the detail live.

questions.stem: A star schema consists of:
options: Many normalised tables in a chain
A central fact table surrounded by denormalised dimension tables
questions.explanation: Deliberately denormalised for query speed and simplicity. A snowflake schema normalises the dimensions further — less redundancy, more joins, slower.

questions.stem: Which best describes the difference between OLTP and OLAP workloads?
options: OLTP handles many small writes to run the business; OLAP handles few large complex reads to analyse the business
OLTP handles few large complex reads; OLAP handles many small writes
Both are identical but on different hardware
OLTP is only for cloud systems
questions.explanation: OLTP: current, detailed, normalised, millisecond response, integrity-focused. OLAP: historical, aggregated, denormalised, seconds-to-minutes, query-speed-focused.

questions.stem: Pre-aggregation in an OLAP layer matters for visualisation because:
options: It reduces the number of charts required
It lets a dashboard respond instantly to drill-down, making the visualisation exploratory rather than a static picture
It removes the need for data cleaning
questions.explanation: Responsiveness changes the kind of thinking a user can do — sub-second answers support a chain of follow-up questions; 30-second answers do not.

questions.stem: A key limitation of relying on a data warehouse for a real-time operations dashboard is:
options: Refresh latency means the warehouse may be hours behind live operations
questions.explanation: Operational monitoring needs a streaming or direct-query path; the warehouse is for integrated historical analysis. Many enterprises run both, which is a genuine architecture trade-off.

questions.stem: Data warehousing supports visualisation of historical trends primarily because it:
options: Deletes old data to save space
Retains years of integrated, conformed history so long-run trend and year-on-year comparison are possible
questions.explanation: "One version of the truth" — every department's chart uses the same definition of the same measure over the same history.

questions.stem: A hidden risk of ETL for the person reading a dashboard is that:
options: Cleaning and transformation decisions made in the pipeline are invisible in the final chart
questions.explanation: Rows excluded, nulls imputed and categories merged during Transform never appear on the visual — which is why provenance and methodology notes belong on serious dashboards.

questions.stem: The four syllabus criteria for data integrity in developing a visualisation are:
questions.explanation: Ownership, source, validation, risk — Build every "assess data integrity" answer on these four. (C) is RAVR — used for assessing data, not the visualisation development process.

questions.stem: In the integrity criterion ownership, the key question is:
options: Who owns or licenses the data, and do you have the right to use and republish it?
questions.explanation: It includes contractual restrictions, third-party licensing and ICIP obligations for Indigenous data — permission to analyse is not automatically permission to publish.

questions.stem: A visualisation is built from a dataset whose schema silently changed at source. This is a failure of:
questions.explanation: A silently renamed or re-typed field produces a chart that still renders and is now wrong — the most dangerous class of error because nothing looks broken.

questions.stem: Poor data quality most directly limits:
options: The scope of visible information and the depth of insight achievable
questions.explanation: Sparse or noisy data forces fewer segments, shorter timeframes and higher aggregation, capping you at descriptive insight with wide error bars.

questions.stem: "Defensive design" in response to low-quality data means:
options: Showing ranges rather than point estimates, annotating caveats, and displaying sample sizes and collection dates
questions.explanation: Honesty about uncertainty is a design decision. A confident-looking point estimate on shaky data is a misleading visualisation even if every number is technically correct.

questions.stem: The syllabus's four lenses on bias in visualisation are:
options: Accuracy, audience, data source, unconscious bias
questions.explanation: Accuracy (errors and systematic omissions), audience (designing to please), data source (single source or shared blind spot) and unconscious bias (the developer's own assumptions).

questions.stem: Bias introduced at the collection stage:
options: Persists and typically compounds through storage, analysis and visualisation
Can be fixed by changing the chart type
questions.explanation: "Bias is never removed by a later stage, only amplified" is the sentence to write in a 6–8 mark question.

questions.stem: A column chart whose y-axis starts at 95 rather than 0 is misleading because:
options: Truncating the axis exaggerates small differences encoded by bar length
The chart type is wrong for the data
questions.explanation: Bars encode value by length, so the baseline must be zero. Line charts, which encode by position and emphasise change, may legitimately use a truncated axis if labelled.

questions.stem: Dual y-axes with independently chosen scales are dangerous because they:
options: Can be scaled to manufacture the appearance of correlation between unrelated series
questions.explanation: The crossing point and apparent tracking are artefacts of the chosen scales. Indexing both series to a common base is the honest alternative.

questions.stem: Scaling a circle's radius rather than its area to a value:
options: Substantially exaggerates large values, because area grows with the square of the radius
questions.explanation: Doubling the radius quadruples the perceived area. Bubble charts must encode value by area.

questions.stem: In a stimulus question, a chart shows sales rising from a start date chosen just after a slump. The technique is:
questions.explanation: Selecting the baseline that flatters the conclusion. The counter is to show the full available series, or annotate why that start point is analytically meaningful.

questions.stem: Which is the most invisible form of editorial control in a visualisation?
options: Filtering — what has been included and excluded
questions.explanation: Readers can see the axis and the colours; they cannot see the records that were silently dropped. Always ask what the filter set is and whether nulls were excluded.

questions.stem: A trend visible in every subgroup reverses when the subgroups are combined. This is:
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox — an aggregation effect. It's the strongest argument for asking what level of aggregation a chart uses before believing its conclusion.

questions.stem: For a 40-million-row dataset requiring live refresh and role-based access, the most appropriate tool category is:
options: Business analytics as a service (Power BI, Tableau)
questions.explanation: Spreadsheets fail past roughly a million rows and lack row-level security; presentation software is a static snapshot. The BI tool's costs — licensing, learning curve, sovereignty — are the balancing points to name.

questions.stem: The chief weakness of presenting data via presentation software is:
options: It is a static snapshot — out of date the moment it is exported, and cannot be interrogated
questions.explanation: Its strengths are narrative control and universal familiarity, which is why it remains right for a one-off executive briefing.

questions.stem: A custom-coded visualisation (e.g. D3.js) is best justified when:
options: The dataset is small and internal
A novel or bespoke visual form is required for a public-facing product, and off-the-shelf tools cannot produce it
questions.explanation: You are buying unlimited flexibility with development cost, timeline, maintenance liability and an accessibility/testing burden that a BI tool would have handled.

questions.stem: Which is a genuine risk of spreadsheet dashboards in an enterprise?
options: They are more expensive than BI tools
Version sprawl — multiple conflicting copies with no single source of truth
questions.explanation: "Which file is current?" is the archetypal spreadsheet governance failure, alongside manual refresh and fragile cross-workbook links.

questions.stem: When justifying a visualisation tool in an exam, the strongest structure is:
options: State explicit criteria (data volume, interactivity, audience skill, update frequency, cost, security, scalability), evaluate options against them, and say why the alternatives are worse
questions.explanation: "Justify" demands argument plus evidence plus rejection of alternatives. Feature lists cap out at half marks.

questions.stem: The five syllabus moves for interrogating a visualisation are:
questions.explanation: Use them as the structure for any stimulus question — they are effectively a mark-scheme in disguise.

questions.stem: When first interrogating a visualisation, you should read:
options: Title, axes, units, scale, legend, source and date before interpreting the shape
The shape of the data first, then the labels
Only the conclusion stated in the caption
questions.explanation: The shape is meaningless without the scale and units. Reading the shape first is exactly how truncated axes fool people.

questions.stem: A single extreme outlier in a scatter plot can:
options: Drag the mean, stretch the axis and create or destroy an apparent trend
questions.explanation: Report the median alongside the mean, show the distribution, and state whether the outlier is an error or a genuine and important extreme.

questions.stem: Which title is the strongest for a dashboard chart?
options: "Sales fell 12% after the July price rise"
questions.explanation: An insight-led title states the finding, not the topic. It removes ambiguity about what the reader is supposed to take away and reduces misinterpretation.

questions.stem: The difference between UX and UI is:
options: UI includes user research; UX does not
UX is the whole quality of the interaction (usefulness, findability, credibility, accessibility); UI is the visual/interactive surface, one part of UX
questions.explanation: A beautiful UI on a dashboard nobody can find the answer in is a UX failure.

questions.stem: Nielsen's heuristic "visibility of system status" applied to a dashboard means:
options: Showing loading indicators and a "last refreshed at" timestamp
questions.explanation: A dashboard that silently serves stale data because a feed failed is worse than one that shows no data at all.

questions.stem: Which Gestalt principle explains why items placed close together are read as a group?
questions.explanation: Proximity — Similarity groups by shared colour or shape; enclosure groups by a shared boundary. Use them deliberately to structure a dashboard rather than relying on borders.

questions.stem: Tufte's data-ink ratio principle recommends:
options: Maximising the proportion of ink devoted to data and removing chartjunk
Using as much decoration as possible
questions.explanation: Chartjunk = heavy gridlines, 3-D, drop shadows, decorative backgrounds, redundant legends. Every removed element makes the remaining data easier to see.

questions.stem: WCAG requires a contrast ratio of at least what for normal-size text?
questions.explanation: 4.5:1 — for normal text at AA (3:1 for large text). Also: never rely on colour alone, provide alt text and a data-table alternative, and ensure keyboard navigability.

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of males have some form of colour vision deficiency, and what design rule follows?
options: ~8% — never encode meaning by colour alone; add labels, patterns or direct annotation
questions.explanation: Roughly 8% of males. Avoid red/green as the sole distinction, use colour-blind-safe palettes, and redundantly encode with position, shape or direct labels.

questions.stem: Placing the most important KPI top-left of a dashboard is justified by:
options: F- and Z-pattern scanning behaviour in left-to-right reading cultures
questions.explanation: Eye-tracking shows readers enter at the top-left and scan in F or Z patterns, so screen position is itself a hierarchy decision.

questions.stem: Responsive design for a dashboard requires:
options: The same layout on every device
Reflowing the layout, reducing elements per screen and using touch targets of at least ~44px
questions.explanation: A desktop dashboard shrunk to phone size is unusable. Mobile layouts should prioritise the two or three metrics that actually drive a decision in the field.

questions.stem: Which is a measurable UX evaluation criterion?
options: "Time to find a specified figure ≤ 30 seconds; task completion rate ≥ 90%; SUS score ≥ 68"
questions.explanation: Criteria must be defined before testing and be measurable. Vague aesthetic goals cannot be evaluated, only asserted.

questions.stem: The best method to discover why users cannot find a figure on a dashboard is:
questions.explanation: Think-aloud reveals the reasoning behind the failure. Analytics tell you that they failed; observation tells you why.

questions.stem: In the visualisation development workflow, discovering at the exploration stage that a field is 40% null should send you:
options: Back to sourcing and preparing data
questions.explanation: The workflow is explicitly iterative — the loops back from exploration to sourcing, and from testing to design, are the point of the diagram.

questions.stem: When incorporating a forecast into a visualisation, best practice is to:
options: Show the forecast as a distinct dashed series with a confidence band, clearly separated from actuals
Show projections in the same style as actuals
Extend the actual line without annotation
questions.explanation: Presenting modelled values as if they were measured is a data-integrity failure. Visual distinction plus an uncertainty band is the honest treatment.

questions.stem: Row-level security in a BI tool means:
options: Users see only the rows they are entitled to see, e.g. their own region's data
questions.explanation: One dashboard, many audiences, enforced at the data layer — far safer than maintaining separate filtered copies per team.

questions.stem: Before publishing an aggregated public dashboard of health data, you should:
options: Publish the raw records for transparency
Suppress small cells that could allow re-identification of individuals
questions.explanation: A cell of "1 case, postcode 2170, aged 15–19" is identifying. Small-cell suppression and aggregation thresholds are standard practice.

questions.stem: The best reason to keep the raw data file untouched and clean a separate copy is:
options: Reproducibility — cleaning decisions can be re-examined, reversed or corrected against the original
questions.explanation: Once you overwrite the raw file, every downstream error becomes permanent and unauditable.

questions.stem: Natural-language query ("show sales by region last quarter") in a BI tool primarily improves:
options: Accessibility of analysis for non-technical users
questions.explanation: It lowers the skill barrier — with the corresponding risk that users get a confident-looking answer to a question the system misinterpreted.

questions.stem: A dashboard shows a KPI in red. A colour-blind user cannot distinguish it. The most appropriate fix is:
options: Add a redundant cue — an icon, label, or explicit "below target" text
questions.explanation: Never rely on colour alone. Redundant encoding preserves the meaning for everyone without removing the visual cue for those who can see it.

questions.stem: An executive asks for "everything on one page". The best UX response is:
options: Include all 40 charts at reduced size
Show the three decision-critical KPIs with trend, and provide drill-through to detail
questions.explanation: Relevance to the audience: an executive needs to know whether to act, not to see every measure. Drill-through preserves access to detail without cognitive overload.

questions.stem: A visualisation shows total complaints falling while complaints per 1,000 customers are rising. The correct interpretation is:
options: The customer base shrank; the rate is the more meaningful measure of service quality
The chart is a Simpson's paradox
questions.explanation: Normalisation changes the story. Raw counts across a changing denominator are the classic comparison error.

questions.stem: A dashboard's "last updated" timestamp reads three days old but the data feed failed a week ago. The design failure is:
options: The system does not degrade gracefully or surface feed failures to the user
questions.explanation: Live analysis carries an obligation to show data health. A silently stale dashboard actively misleads decision-makers who believe it is current.

questions.stem: In evaluating a completed dashboard against criteria, the strongest answer structure is:
options: State the criterion → state the evidence/measurement → make a judgement → note the limitation → recommend an improvement
Compare it to a competitor's dashboard
questions.explanation: "Evaluate" requires a judgement against criteria supported by evidence, with balance. Description alone is a band-3 answer.

questions.stem: Blending live operational data with warehouse history on one dashboard enables:
options: Comparison of today's performance against the historical baseline, flagging deviation in real time
Removal of the need for cleaning
questions.explanation: "Today vs the same day last year" is only possible because the warehouse retains conformed history alongside the live feed.

questions.stem: A council publishes a choropleth of "reported graffiti incidents" per suburb. A significant interpretive caution is:
options: The map uses too many colours
It maps reporting behaviour as much as incidence — suburbs with engaged residents report more
questions.explanation: Passive-collection datasets record the act of reporting, not the underlying phenomenon. This is measurement bias at the collection stage, carried into the visual.

questions.stem: A retailer wants a dashboard used by store managers on the shop floor. The most important design decision is:
options: Mobile-responsive layout with few, decision-relevant metrics and large touch targets
questions.explanation: Design follows the persona and the context of use — standing, glancing, on a phone, mid-shift.

questions.stem: Which combination of applications is the most coherent pipeline for a recurring forecast dashboard?
options: SQL database → Power Query ETL → forecasting model → Power BI dashboard
questions.explanation: Each tool does what it is best at: the database stores and secures, ETL cleans, the model forecasts, the BI layer communicates. The cost is integration complexity and more failure points.

questions.stem: A visualisation is accurate, attractive and unused. In an evaluation this should be judged:
options: A failure against the criterion of communicating to the audience — an unused visualisation delivers no value
Successful, because the data is correct
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is measured by whether it supports a decision. Adoption, task success and acted-on insights are legitimate evaluation criteria.

questions.stem: The main visualisation argument for normalising to an index (e.g. base year = 100) is:
options: It makes series of very different magnitudes comparable in terms of relative change
It converts data to ratio level
questions.explanation: It is also the honest alternative to a dual-axis chart, which manufactures apparent correlation through arbitrary scaling.

questions.stem: A dashboard designer adds 12 filters "for flexibility". The likely UX consequence is:
options: Choice overload and inconsistent results between users; better to provide sensible defaults with fewer, meaningful filters
questions.explanation: Customisation gives ownership but adds complexity. Defaults are a design decision — most users never change them, so the default view is the product.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that a visualisation improved a business outcome?
options: A measured change in the KPI the visualisation was designed to influence, compared against a baseline or control
The chart uses the brand palette
questions.explanation: Outcome evidence beats output evidence. Views measure attention; the KPI measures effect.

questions.stem: An analyst presents a correlation of 0.85 as proof that advertising drives sales. The best critique is:
options: Correlation does not establish causation — reverse causation and confounders (seasonality, price changes, competitor activity) must be excluded
The sample must be a census
questions.explanation: Advertising spend often follows expected demand, making reverse causation entirely plausible. Controlled experiments or A/B tests are what establish causality.

questions.stem: Which visualisation decision most improves credibility with a sceptical audience?
options: Citing the source, collection date, sample size and methodology directly on the visual
Removing the axis labels for cleanliness
questions.explanation: Provenance on the face of the chart pre-empts the first question a sceptical reader asks and signals that the analysis will survive scrutiny.

questions.stem: A live streaming dashboard refreshing every second for a metric that changes monthly is:
options: Poor design — refresh frequency should match the decision cadence, and over-refreshing adds cost and cognitive noise
questions.explanation: Refresh rate is a design decision balancing decision timeliness against infrastructure cost and user distraction.

questions.stem: In a stimulus question showing a chart with no y-axis label, the correct first observation is:
options: Without units and scale the magnitude of the change cannot be judged, so no conclusion about significance can be drawn
questions.explanation: Missing units is one of the listed misleading techniques. Say what cannot be concluded — that's the analytical move markers reward.

questions.stem: An enterprise reports "conversions up 300%". The most important missing context is:
options: The base — 300% of what absolute number, and over what timeframe
The tool used to build the chart
questions.explanation: Percentages without a base are one of the classic misleading techniques: 1 → 4 conversions is a 300% increase and commercially meaningless.

questions.stem: VR/AR data environments are most defensible in an enterprise when:
options: The data is two-dimensional and simple
Spatial context genuinely adds meaning — e.g. AR overlays of sensor data on a factory floor
questions.explanation: Novelty is not a justification. The test is whether immersion improves the decision compared to a well-designed 2-D view.

questions.stem: The strongest reason to run an accessibility audit before deploying a public dashboard is:
options: Legal compliance obligations and the exclusion of users who otherwise cannot access public information
questions.explanation: Accessibility is both a legal and an ethical obligation — and remediation after launch is far more expensive than designing to WCAG from the start.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of using visualisation for exploration rather than explanation?
options: An analyst cross-filtering a scatter matrix to find which variables relate before forming a hypothesis
A polished infographic for a media release
questions.explanation: Exploration is analyst-facing, fast, ugly and iterative. Explanation is audience-facing, curated and polished. Confusing the two produces cluttered dashboards and shallow reports.

questions.stem: A dashboard aggregates results to the national level. A regional manager complains it is useless. The best design response is:
options: Add drill-down and role-based default filters so each user lands on their own region with the ability to roll up
questions.explanation: One well-modelled dataset with drill-down and row-level security serves many personas without version sprawl.

questions.stem: In an 8-mark question on bias in a visualisation, the strongest structure names:
options: The stage at which bias entered (collection, storage, analysis, visualisation), the mechanism, its effect on the conclusion, and a mitigation — with a judgement
questions.explanation: Pointing to the stage and the mechanism demonstrates analysis rather than description, and gives a natural four-paragraph structure.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible criterion set for evaluating a completed enterprise dashboard?
options: Accuracy vs source, task completion rate, time to insight, accessibility conformance, adoption/usage, and measured effect on the target KPI
questions.explanation: Measurable, pre-defined and tied to purpose. State the criteria explicitly in the answer before you evaluate against them.

questions.stem: The single most important thing a visualisation developer can do to protect data integrity is:
options: Document provenance, cleaning decisions and definitions, and validate outputs against an independent source
questions.explanation: Integrity is a process, not a property of the image. Traceability from the number on the chart back to the source record is what makes a visualisation defensible.
